drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97 (+3.7%)
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at $3.97 saw median x0.85 and x0.60 vs baseline; noise-adjusted effect of price hikes is x0.85. No prior data on heatwaves, so no uplift.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.2. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price is raised by 3.7% (to $3.97), which historically correlates with demand drops: recent week at $3.97 (2026-09-28) sold 106 units (x0.85 vs baseline), and the following week (2026-10-05) sold 75 units (x0.60). The heatwave forecast (38°C) may boost demand for cold snacks, but no past heatwave data is available. The noise-adjusted effect of a price increase is x0.85, and the baseline already reflects seasonal trends. No historical uplift from heatwaves. The classical model suggests no effect, but we adjust for price. The evidence for price impact is strong (2 recent weeks at same price), so we apply a downward adjustment. No other drivers. Confidence is medium.

PRODUCT: Tortilla Chips 300g | category Snacks | Store #12 (Austin, TX)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: Heatwave forecast: 38°C all week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.7 - 200.1 | 10%-90%: 89.1 - 170.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
